lessons.title: Growth and Development of the Foal
lessons.body: A newborn foal should stand within 1-2 hours and nurse within 2-4 hours. If it doesn't, call a vet immediately. In the first month, a foal gains 0.5-1 kg per day. By 6 months, it should weigh about 45-50% of its mature weight. Measure weight using a weigh tape around the heart girth; if you don't have one, estimate by heart girth in centimeters: weight (kg) â (heart girth cm)^2.6 / 11,000. For example, a foal with a 100 cm girth weighs about 100^2.6/11000 â 110 kg. Record weight weekly. Height at withers also increases rapidly: about 1 cm per week for the first 3 months. Use a measuring stick or a marked wall. Monitor growth rate; if a foal gains less than 0.4 kg/day after the first month, increase feed or check for parasites. In Africa, rapid growth in hot climates can cause stress; provide shade and fresh water. The foal's legs are long at birth, making them appear awkward. This is normal. By 3 months, the foal will start eating solid food, but milk is still the main diet until 4-6 months. Observe the foal's body condition: ribs should be felt but not seen. If ribs are visible, the foal is too thin; if ribs cannot be felt, it's too fat. Adjust feed accordingly. Keep records of weight and height to spot problems early. A healthy foal is alert, curious, and plays frequently. If it lies down a lot or seems dull, it may be sick. Deworm every 4-6 weeks starting at 2 months of age using a product like ivermectin at 0.2 mg/kg body weight. Also, ensure the foal gets colostrum in the first 6 hours for immunity. Without colostrum, the foal is at high risk of infection. If the mare rejects the foal, milk her and bottle-feed the colostrum. In Africa, many smallholders have local breeds; these may grow slower but are hardy. Adjust expectations accordingly. Focus on steady, consistent growth rather than maximum speed.

lessons.title: Nutritional Management of the Growing Foal
lessons.body: From birth to 3 months, the foal gets most nutrition from mare's milk. A good mare produces 10-20 liters of milk per day. To support this, feed the mare 2-3 kg of concentrate daily plus good hay and pasture. If the mare is thin, increase feed. The foal will start nibbling at 1-2 weeks. Provide a creep feederâa small pen with feed that only the foal can enter. Use a creep feed with 16-18% protein, 0.8-1.0% calcium, and 0.5-0.7% phosphorus. A simple mix: 50% crushed maize, 30% soybean meal, 15% wheat bran, 5% mineral-vitamin premix. Add salt at 0.5%. Feed 0.5-1 kg per day at 2 months, increasing to 2-3 kg by 6 months. Split into 2-3 meals. Always provide clean water. In hot African climates, foals drink 20-30 liters per day. If pasture is poor, give good-quality hay (e.g., lucerne or Rhodes grass) free-choice. Avoid sudden feed changes; introduce new feed over 7-10 days. Watch for diarrhea; if it occurs, reduce concentrate and add probiotics. Weigh the foal monthly to adjust feed: a 6-month-old foal should eat about 1-1.5% of its body weight in concentrate plus hay. For a 200 kg foal, that's 2-3 kg concentrate. If the foal is too thin, increase by 0.5 kg per day. If too fat, reduce. Minerals are critical: calcium and phosphorus in a 2:1 ratio. A lack causes bone problems. Provide a mineral block or loose minerals. In Africa, many soils are deficient in selenium and copper; use a supplement with 0.3 ppm selenium and 10 ppm copper. Also, add vitamin E. If the foal is orphaned, use a mare milk replacer (e.g., Foal Lac) at 10-20% of body weight per day, divided into 6-8 feedings. Never feed cow's milk alone; it causes diarrhea. Gradually introduce solid feed by 2 weeks. By 6 months, the foal should eat 2-3 kg concentrate and 2-3 kg hay daily. Adjust based on body condition. Keep feed troughs clean to prevent mold. Aflatoxin in maize can kill foals. Buy from trusted suppliers.

lessons.title: Handling and Early Training of Foals
lessons.body: Start handling the foal within the first 24-48 hours. Wear gloves and move slowly. Approach the mare first, then the foal. Touch the foal all over: head, neck, back, legs, and hooves. This makes future trimming and vet care easier. Use a soft cotton rope halter; don't use a chain. Put it on and off several times a day for short periods. Reward with gentle scratching. By 1 week, teach the foal to lead with a butt rope. Stand on the foal's left side, hold the halter with your right hand and a rope behind its rump with your left. Ask it to walk forward; never pull. Use a calm voice. Practice for 5-10 minutes daily. By 1 month, the foal should tie quietly for 10 minutes. Use a quick-release knot. Never leave a tied foal unsupervised. Pick up feet daily: start with front, then back. Hold each foot for a few seconds, then release. Gradually increase to 30 seconds. This prevents kicking later. By 3 months, introduce grooming with a soft brush. Also, teach the foal to stand for the farrier; have the farrier visit monthly just to handle the feet. In Africa, many foals are not handled until weaning, which makes them wild. Invest time daily. Use a small pen or stable for training. Avoid shouting or hitting; it creates fear. If the foal resists, stay calm and patient. Use food rewards like a handful of concentrate. By 6 months, the foal should walk, trot, and stop on command. Also, get it used to a trailer: park a trailer in the yard, feed the foal near it, then inside. This reduces stress when transporting. Handle the foal's ears and mouth; this helps with deworming and dental care. Introduce clippers and spray bottles. For African conditions, also get the foal used to flies and heat; apply fly spray and provide shade. Socialize the foal with other horses, but avoid aggressive ones. A well-handled foal becomes a safe adult horse. Spend 15-20 minutes daily. Consistency is key. If you have multiple foals, handle each individually. Record progress. If a foal is difficult, seek help from an experienced handler. Never use force; it damages trust.

lessons.title: Weaning Methods and Timing
lessons.body: Weaning is the process of separating the foal from the mare. The best time is 4-6 months, when the foal is eating 1-2 kg of concentrate daily and can survive without milk. In Africa, wean during the cool dry season to reduce stress. Never wean before 3 months; the foal's immune system is not ready. Methods: abrupt separation, gradual separation, and fence-line weaning. Abrupt: move the mare to a distant paddock where the foal cannot see or hear her. This causes stress and possible injury. Not recommended. Gradual: separate for increasing periods over 1-2 weeks. Start with 1 hour, then 2, then 4, then overnight. Finally, separate permanently. This is kinder. Fence-line: put the mare and foal in adjacent paddocks with a strong fence. They can see and touch but not nurse. After 3-5 days, move the mare further away. This is the best method for smallholders. Whichever method, reduce the mare's feed 2 days before weaning to lower milk production and prevent mastitis. Check her udder daily for heat or hardness; if present, milk her out and call a vet. For the foal, provide a clean, safe pen with hay and water. Feed the same concentrate it was eating before weaning. Offer small meals 3-4 times daily. Monitor the foal's weight; some loss is normal (up to 5% in first week). If it loses more than 10%, consult a vet. The foal should be dewormed and vaccinated before weaning. After weaning, keep the foal in a small group with other weanlings for company. In Africa, many farmers wean at 8-12 months, which is too late; it drains the mare and reduces her fertility. Aim for 6 months. If the mare is pregnant again, wean by 5 months. Use a halter and lead rope to move the foal gently. Never chase. After weaning, the mare may call for 2-3 days; this is normal. Give her plenty of water and hay. Watch for mastitis. The foal may also call; provide distractions like toys or a companion. Within a week, both settle. Record weaning date and weight. If you have limited space, wean one foal at a time. Always ensure the foal has been eating solid feed well before weaning. A foal that is not eating enough will struggle. Weaning is stressful but necessary for the mare's health and the foal's independence.

lessons.title: Health Care and Vaccination Schedules
lessons.body: Foals need a strong health program. First, ensure they get colostrum within 6 hours of birth. If not, give 1 liter of frozen colostrum or plasma. Vaccinate the mare 4-6 weeks before foaling with tetanus, influenza, and herpes (EHV-1/4). This boosts colostrum quality. For the foal: at 3 months, start vaccinations. Give tetanus toxoid (1 ml IM) and influenza (1 ml IM). Repeat in 4 weeks. At 6 months, give rabies (2 ml IM) and African horse sickness (AHS) if in endemic areas (1 ml SC). AHS vaccine is live; give only in areas where the disease occurs. Also, deworm: at 2 months, use fenbendazole (5 mg/kg) or ivermectin (0.2 mg/kg). Repeat every 4-6 weeks until 6 months, then every 8 weeks. In Africa, ticks are a major problem. Use tick grease or spray with amitraz every 2 weeks. Check for tick-borne diseases like piroplasmosis; signs are fever, jaundice, and colic. Treat with imidocarb (2.2 mg/kg SC). Also, watch for diarrhea. In foals, diarrhea can be caused by rotavirus, Salmonella, or parasites. If diarrhea lasts more than 24 hours, call a vet. Give oral electrolytes. For respiratory disease, vaccinate against strangles (Streptococcus equi) at 4 months and 6 months (1 ml IM). Also, deworm for bots in autumn. Hoof care: trim every 4-6 weeks. If the foal is lame, check for abscess. In hot climates, provide shade and fresh water to prevent heat stress. Vaccinate against anthrax in endemic areas (1 ml SC annually). Keep records. A simple notebook with dates and products. If you cannot afford all vaccines, prioritize tetanus and rabies. Tetanus kills; rabies is zoonotic. Also, test for equine infectious anemia (EIA) annually; in many African countries, it's required for movement. Use sterile needles and dispose safely. Never reuse needles. For deworming, rotate products to prevent resistance. Use a weigh tape to dose accurately. Underdosing leads to resistance. If a foal is sick, isolate it. Common signs: dullness, not eating, fever (over 38.5Â°C), diarrhea, cough. Take temperature rectally with a digital thermometer. Normal is 37.5-38.5Â°C. If fever, call a vet. Keep a first-aid kit: bandages, antiseptic, scissors, thermometer, gloves. In Africa, many vets are far; learn basic skills. Attend a training workshop. Prevention is cheaper than treatment.

lessons.title: Preventing Developmental Orthopedic Diseases
lessons.body: Developmental orthopedic diseases (DOD) are bone and joint problems in growing foals. Common types: osteochondrosis (OCD), physitis, angular limb deformities, and contracted tendons. Causes include rapid growth, unbalanced nutrition, genetics, and trauma. To prevent DOD, control growth rate. Aim for moderate, steady growth, not maximum. A foal should gain 0.5-0.8 kg per day, not more. Feed a balanced diet with correct calcium:phosphorus ratio (2:1). Avoid high-energy feeds like straight maize; they cause rapid growth. Use a concentrate with 16% protein and added minerals. Provide free-choice hay. Do not overfeed. Keep the foal's body condition score at 5 out of 9 (ribs easily felt, not visible). Exercise is important: allow free movement in a paddock daily. Confinement increases DOD risk. In Africa, many foals are kept in small pens; provide at least 100 square meters per foal. If not possible, hand-walk for 30 minutes daily. Avoid strenuous exercise like lunging or chasing. Also, avoid excessive trauma: don't let foals run on hard, rocky ground. Check hooves regularly. Angular limb deformities: if the foal's legs are crooked, consult a vet early. Mild cases correct with trimming. Severe cases need surgery. Contracted tendons: if the foal walks on its toes, provide a soft bed and gentle stretching. If it cannot stand, call a vet. Physitis: swollen growth plates above the hooves. Rest and reduce feed. In all cases, early detection is key. Weigh and measure the foal monthly. If growth is too fast, reduce concentrate by 20%. If too slow, increase by 10%. Also, ensure copper and zinc levels are adequate. In Africa, many soils are deficient; supplement with 10 mg copper and 40 mg zinc per kg feed. Selenium is also needed: 0.3 ppm. Vitamin E: 100 IU per day. Avoid excess phosphorus; it causes bone weakness. Use a mineral premix designed for horses. Do not feed dog or chicken feed. If DOD occurs, work with a vet. X-rays may be needed. Treatment includes rest, corrective trimming, and sometimes surgery. But prevention is far cheaper. Keep records of growth and feed. If a foal has a history of DOD, adjust its diet and exercise. Genetics play a role; avoid breeding from affected horses. In Africa, many local breeds are hardy, but crossbreeds may be more susceptible. Monitor closely. Share knowledge with other farmers. A healthy foal is a sound future horse.

quiz.q: How soon after birth should a foal stand and nurse?
quiz.explanation: A healthy foal should stand within 1-2 hours and nurse within 2-4 hours; 6 hours is the maximum acceptable delay.

quiz.q: What is the approximate daily weight gain for a foal in the first month?
quiz.explanation: Foals typically gain 0.5-1 kg per day in the first month.

quiz.q: How can you estimate a foal's weight without a scale?
quiz.explanation: Heart girth measurement using a weigh tape or formula gives a good estimate.

quiz.q: What is the recommended protein percentage in creep feed for foals?
quiz.explanation: Creep feed should contain 16-18% protein for growing foals.

quiz.q: What is the ideal calcium to phosphorus ratio in a foal's diet?
quiz.explanation: A 2:1 calcium to phosphorus ratio is correct for bone development.

quiz.q: How much concentrate should a 6-month-old foal eat per day?
quiz.explanation: By 6 months, a foal should eat 2-3 kg of concentrate daily.

quiz.q: What should you do if a foal has diarrhea after eating concentrate?
options: B) Reduce concentrate and add probiotics
quiz.explanation: Reduce concentrate and add probiotics to manage diarrhea.

quiz.q: When should you start handling a foal?
quiz.explanation: Start handling within the first 24-48 hours for best results.

quiz.q: What type of halter is best for a young foal?
quiz.explanation: A soft cotton halter is gentle and safe for a foal.

quiz.q: How long should you practice leading a foal daily?
quiz.explanation: Short, frequent sessions of 5-10 minutes are effective and prevent stress.

quiz.q: What is the best method for weaning a foal in a smallholder setting?
quiz.explanation: Fence-line weaning reduces stress by allowing sight and touch but preventing nursing.

quiz.q: At what age is it best to wean a foal?
quiz.explanation: Weaning at 4-6 months is ideal when the foal is eating solid feed well.

quiz.q: What should you do to the mare's feed before weaning?
quiz.explanation: Reduce the mare's feed 2 days before weaning to lower milk production and prevent mastitis.

quiz.q: What is a sign of mastitis in the mare after weaning?
quiz.explanation: A hard, hot udder indicates mastitis; milk her out and call a vet.

quiz.q: When should a foal receive its first vaccinations?
quiz.explanation: Start vaccinations at 3 months of age, as maternal antibodies decline.

quiz.q: Which vaccine is a priority if you cannot afford all?
quiz.explanation: Tetanus is a deadly disease and vaccination is a priority.

quiz.q: How often should you deworm a foal from 2 to 6 months?
quiz.explanation: Deworm every 4-6 weeks from 2 to 6 months of age.

quiz.q: What is the normal rectal temperature for a foal?
quiz.explanation: Normal temperature is 37.5-38.5Â°C.

quiz.q: What is a common sign of tick-borne disease in foals?
quiz.explanation: Jaundice is a sign of piroplasmosis, a tick-borne disease.

quiz.q: What is the best way to prevent developmental orthopedic diseases?
quiz.explanation: Controlling growth rate to moderate, steady gain prevents DOD.

quiz.q: What is a sign of physitis in a foal?
options: A) Swollen growth plates above hooves
quiz.explanation: Physitis causes swelling at the growth plates above the hooves.

quiz.q: How much space should a foal have for exercise to prevent DOD?
quiz.explanation: At least 100 square meters per foal for free movement.

quiz.q: What mineral is often deficient in African soils and important for bone health?
quiz.explanation: Copper deficiency is common and can lead to DOD.

quiz.q: What should you do if a foal shows signs of contracted tendons?
options: B) Provide soft bed and gentle stretching
quiz.explanation: Soft bedding and gentle stretching help mild contracted tendons.

quiz.q: What is the recommended selenium level in a foal's supplement?
quiz.explanation: 0.3 ppm selenium is adequate and safe.

quiz.q: How often should you trim a foal's hooves?
quiz.explanation: Hooves should be trimmed every 4-6 weeks.

quiz.q: What is the first step in handling a newborn foal?
quiz.explanation: Start by touching the foal all over to desensitize it.

quiz.q: What is a creep feeder?
options: B) A small pen for foals to eat
quiz.explanation: A creep feeder allows foals to eat concentrate without competition.

quiz.q: What is the best time of year to wean in Africa?
quiz.explanation: Wean during the cool dry season to reduce stress.

quiz.q: What should you do if a foal loses more than 10% of its body weight after weaning?
quiz.explanation: Excessive weight loss after weaning requires veterinary advice.
